entities.summary:
Bérard de Got (c. 1250 – July 4, 1297) was a prominent French prelate who ascended to the highest ranks of the Roman Catholic Church, serving as Archbishop of Lyon from 1289 and later as Cardinal-Bishop of Albano from 1294 until his death. His career unfolded during a period of intense political and ecclesiastical maneuvering in late 13th-century Western Europe, marked by the growing assertiveness of the French monarchy and the evolving power dynamics within the papacy. As the son of Bérard, Lord of Villandraut, and elder brother to Bertrand de Got, who would later become Pope Clement V, Bérard's influence stemmed from both his personal ecclesiastical appointments and his family's burgeoning prominence in Gascony.

Elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Celestine V on September 18, 1294, Bérard de Got became Cardinal-Bishop of Albano, a pivotal role within the College of Cardinals. Prior to this, he had held the influential archiepiscopal see of Lyon, a key ecclesiastical and political center in the Kingdom of France, from 1289. His service spanned the pontificates of Nicholas IV, the brief, reform-minded reign of Celestine V, and the contentious early years of Boniface VIII. During these transitions, Bérard participated in the complex papal elections, including the one that controversially elevated Boniface VIII after Celestine V's unprecedented abdication, navigating the volatile political landscape between French royal interests and papal authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Bérard de Got's trajectory as Archbishop of Lyon and Cardinal-Bishop of Albano placed him at the core of late 13th-century papal politics and French ecclesiastical power, contributing to the dynastic rise that would see his brother become Pope Clement V. His career offers a window into the complex interplay of family influence, church office, and national interests.
